title: AUD U3·W1 — Auditing in an IT Environment: ITGCs, Application Controls & Data Analytics
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the ledger lives in a system

MBG's general ledger, payroll, and job-cost records live in software, so the auditor cannot evaluate controls without evaluating the information technology that runs them. This week covers the two layers of IT control — general and application — the techniques for testing controls inside a system, the rise of audit data analytics, and the SOC reports that let an auditor rely on a service organization. It extends the internal-control foundation from AUD Unit 1 into the systems where the data actually lives.

General IT controls

IT general controls (ITGCs) are the pervasive controls over the IT environment that make application controls trustworthy. They fall into four areas: access security (logical access, passwords, segregation of incompatible duties in the system), program change management (authorizing, testing, and approving changes to software), program development (controls over acquiring and implementing new systems), and computer operations (job scheduling, backup, recovery). Weak ITGCs undermine every application control they support — if a programmer can change code without approval, no automated control can be relied upon.

Application controls

Application controls operate within a specific process to ensure transactions are complete, accurate, and authorized. They are classified by stage: input controls (validation and edit checks, such as a field that rejects a non-numeric invoice amount, or a check digit), processing controls (batch totals, run-to-run reconciliations, limit and reasonableness tests), and output controls (distribution restrictions, output reconciliation). An automated application control can be tested once for design and a single operation, provided the supporting ITGCs establish that the program did not change during the period — the efficiency payoff of a strong IT environment.

Testing controls inside the system

To test automated controls, the auditor uses computer-assisted techniques. The test-data approach runs the auditor's fictitious transactions — including deliberately invalid ones — through the client's program to see whether controls catch them. An integrated test facility embeds a dummy entity in the live system, and parallel simulation reprocesses real data through the auditor's own program and compares results. Generalized audit software (GAS) reads client data files to recompute, summarize, and test — extracting exceptions the auditor then investigates. These CAATs turn the system from an obstacle into a testing tool.

The reliance decision

The IT evaluation feeds the same audit-risk logic as Unit 1. If ITGCs and application controls are designed and operating effectively, the auditor can assess control risk below maximum and reduce substantive testing. If ITGCs are weak, the auditor cannot rely on automated controls and must shift to a substantive strategy — testing the outputs directly with more extensive procedures. In a highly automated environment, a purely substantive approach may even be impossible (no paper trail), forcing reliance on controls and making the IT evaluation mandatory rather than optional.

Audit data analytics

Audit data analytics (ADAs) apply analysis to entire populations rather than samples, surfacing relationships and anomalies. Uses span the audit: risk assessment (visualizing revenue by location to spot outliers), tests of details (matching every shipment to an invoice), and the required journal-entry testing for fraud (filtering for round-dollar, post-period, or unusual-user entries). ADAs do not replace professional judgment — every flagged item is a notable item to evaluate, not automatically a misstatement — but they let the auditor cover 100% of a population where sampling once covered a fraction.

Service organizations and SOC reports

When MBG outsources a process — payroll to a provider, hosting to a cloud vendor — the relevant controls sit at the service organization. Under AU-C 402, the user auditor obtains a SOC 1 report (controls relevant to user financial reporting) prepared by the service auditor. A Type 1 report opines on the design of controls at a point in time; a Type 2 report also tests operating effectiveness over a period — so only a Type 2 supports the user auditor's reliance on those controls. SOC 2 reports address security, availability, confidentiality, and privacy for broader stakeholders, and complementary user-entity controls remind the user that some controls remain its own responsibility.

Cybersecurity and data integrity

The auditor also considers how cybersecurity risk could affect the financial statements — a breach that corrupts data, triggers a contingent liability, or impairs going concern. While a financial-statement audit is not a cybersecurity audit, the auditor evaluates relevant controls over data integrity and remains alert to the financial-reporting consequences of an incident. The reliability of every number the audit touches ultimately rests on whether the systems that produced it were secure and controlled.

Segregation of duties in a computerized system

In a manual system, duties are separated among people; in an IT system, the same principle applies to access rights. The auditor verifies that no individual holds incompatible logical access — for example, the ability to both create a vendor and approve a payment, or to both write program code and move it into production. Privileged access (system and database administrators) is especially sensitive because it can override application controls, so it is restricted, logged, and reviewed. Where the entity is too small to separate duties, the auditor looks for compensating controls such as detailed management review of system logs and exception reports.

End-user computing and spreadsheets

Material figures often flow through spreadsheets built outside the formal IT environment — a depreciation schedule, a percentage-of-completion calculation, a consolidation worksheet. These end-user computing tools fall outside ITGCs, so they carry elevated risk of formula errors, broken links, and unauthorized changes. The auditor tests the spreadsheet's logic and integrity directly — re-performing key formulas, checking that ranges are complete, and confirming version control — because a single wrong cell reference can misstate a material balance just as surely as a coding error in the core system.

Continuous auditing and the audit trail

Automation also reshapes when the auditor works. Continuous auditing techniques — embedded audit modules and exception flags that capture transactions as they occur — let the auditor monitor controls throughout the period rather than only at year-end. The premise of all of it is a reliable audit trail: the system must log enough detail (who, what, when) to trace any balance back to its source transactions. Where the trail is electronic and short-lived, the auditor plans procedures to capture evidence before it is overwritten, because lost data cannot be re-created after the fact.

CMA bridge

CMA month 6 built the internal-control and systems perspective for MBG; AUD applies it from the auditor's chair — testing the ITGCs and application controls that management designed. The same job-cost system MBG uses to accumulate WIP is what the auditor must evaluate before relying on a single automated cost figure.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify ITGCs (access, change management, development, operations) and recognize that weak ITGCs undermine the application controls they support.
  2. Identify application controls by stage (input edit checks/check digits, processing batch totals, output controls).
  3. Apply CAATs — test data, integrated test facility, parallel simulation, generalized audit software — and use ADAs for full-population and journal-entry testing.
  4. Distinguish SOC 1 Type 1 (design) from Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period); only Type 2 supports reliance.

Recap: auditing in an IT environment means evaluating ITGCs (access, change, development, operations) that make application controls (input/processing/output) reliable; testing them with CAATs like test data, parallel simulation, and generalized audit software; using audit data analytics for full-population and fraud journal-entry testing; and obtaining a SOC 1 Type 2 report — operating effectiveness over a period — before relying on a service organization's controls.

flashcards.back: Pervasive controls: access security, program change management, program development, and computer operations. Weak ITGCs undermine every application control they support.
Process-level controls by stage: input (edit checks, check digits), processing (batch totals, reconciliations), output (distribution/reconciliation).
Test data: run auditor's fictitious transactions through the client's program. Parallel simulation: reprocess real client data through the auditor's own program and compare.
Software that reads client data files to recompute, summarize, and extract exceptions for the auditor to investigate.
Analysis of entire populations (not samples) for risk assessment, tests of details, and fraud journal-entry testing; flagged items are 'notable items' to evaluate.
Type 1: design of controls at a point in time. Type 2: design AND operating effectiveness over a period. Only Type 2 supports the user auditor's reliance.
Controls the SOC report assumes the user organization itself performs; reliance on the service org's controls depends on them.
In a highly automated, paperless environment a purely substantive approach may be impossible, forcing reliance on (and testing of) controls.

questions.q: If IT general controls are weak, the auditor should:
choices: Not rely on automated application controls and increase substantive testing
Rely fully on application controls anyway
questions.explain: Weak ITGCs undermine the application controls they support, so the auditor cannot rely on them.

questions.q: A check digit on an account number is an example of a(n):
questions.explain: Check digits validate data at entry — an input application control.

questions.q: Reprocessing actual client data through the auditor's own program and comparing results is:
questions.explain: Parallel simulation reruns real data through the auditor's program; test data runs fictitious transactions through the client's program.

questions.q: Which SOC 1 report supports the user auditor's reliance on a service organization's controls?
choices: Type 1 (design at a point in time)
questions.explain: Only a Type 2 report tests operating effectiveness over a period, supporting reliance.

questions.q: Audit data analytics differ from sampling because they:
questions.explain: ADAs analyze whole populations; flagged 'notable items' still require auditor judgment.

questions.q: Required journal-entry testing for fraud commonly filters for:
questions.explain: Fraud journal-entry testing targets unusual characteristics like round amounts, post-period dates, and odd preparers.

choices: Controls the user organization itself must perform for the service org's controls to be effective
questions.explain: A SOC report assumes certain controls operate at the user entity; reliance depends on them.
